scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The choreography for the Česká beseda was created in 1862 and 1863 by Prague dance master Karel Link at the request of writer Jan Neruda.
Ferdinand Heller composed the music using traditional folk and dance melodies, with Bedřich Smetana also assisting in its creation.
It premiered in November 1863 at a social evening in Prague's Konviktsaal danced by 24 pairs, and was performed by 140 pairs on Sofia Island in January 1864, rapidly spreading across Bohemia.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The term 'beseda' originally means a chat or conversation in Czech, extending to a social gathering or evening of entertainment.
Events featuring besedas were organized with great success starting in the 1840s to enliven social life and strengthen national consciousness.
Today, the Česká beseda is performed mainly at folkloristic events.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by four pairs who stand opposite each other in a cross-shaped quadrille formation.
It lasts approximately 12 minutes and is structured into four parts (figures), each containing two sections.
The first section stands in 3/4 time and ends with a 16-bar furiant, while the second section is in 2/4 time.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music was composed by Ferdinand Heller, incorporating traditional folk and dance melodies with short overtures introducing each part.
It features contrasting meters, alternating between 3/4 time (concluding with characteristic furiants marked by rapid tempos, hemiolas, and syncopation) and 2/4 time.
The pulse is 3/4 and 2/4.
Orchestral salon music utilizing traditional Bohemian folk and dance melodies, alternating between lyrical 3/4 movements ending in energetic furiants with hemiolas and lively 2/4 sections.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures involved in the creation and popularization of the Česká beseda include dance master Karel Link, composer Ferdinand Heller, writer Jan Neruda, and composer Bedřich Smetana, all of whom participated in its early development and premiere.

Following the success of the original Bohemian Česká beseda, similar composite beseda dances emerged in later years based on the traditional dances of specific regions, resulting in the Moravian (Moravská), Hanakian (Hanácká), and Silesian (Slezská) besedas.
Classified as a subclass of Czech folk dance and structured as a traditional Bohemian salon dance in the style of a court quadrille (quadrille à la cour).
